title: TWO ANTARCTIC SITES, THE YAMATO MOUNTAINS BLUE-ICE METEORITE FIELD AND THE NAPIER COMPLEX IN ENDERBY LAND, HAVE BEEN INCLUDED IN THE THIRD 100 IUGS GEOLOGICAL HERITAGE SITES > National Institute of Polar Research
excerpt: TWO ANTARCTIC SITES, THE YAMATO MOUNTAINS BLUE-ICE METEORITE FIELD AND THE NAPIER COMPLEX IN ENDERBY LAND, HAVE BEEN INCLUDED IN THE THIRD 100 IUGS GEOLOGICAL HERITAGE SITES
content:
November 24, 2026

The International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) has selected two sites in Antarctica for inclusion in the Third 100 IUGS Geological Heritage Sites: the Yamato Mountains blue-ice meteorite field and Archean Ultrahigh Temperature Metamorphism in the Napier Complex.

IUGS Geological Heritage Sites are selected by the International Union of Geological Sciences on the basis of their outstanding scientific value as exceptional examples of geological features, processes and discoveries. They represent some of the world’s most significant places for understanding the Earth and its history. Located across the globe, they offer an unsurpassed journey through the most important geological sites of the Earth.

The blue-ice areas around the Yamato Mountains are one of the world's largest meteorite concentration sites, with approximately 14,000 meteorites recovered to date. The discovery of meteorites in this region by the 10th Japanese Antarctic Research Expedition (JARE) in 1969 led to the recognition of Antarctica as a major repository of meteorites and helped reveal the mechanism of meteorite concentration through the flow of ice sheets. The site's outstanding number of recovered meteorites, their petrological and geochemical diversity, its historical significance, and the scientific contributions made through decades of research by JARE were recognised in its selection.

The Napier Complex, located in Enderby Land, East Antarctica, includes areas such as Tonagh Island and Mount Riiser-Larsen. It has been included in this prestigious list because it is recognised internationally, thanks to seminal studies by Australian National Antarctic Research Expeditions (ANARE) geologists and further investigations by geoscientists from JARE, as the premier example of and type area for ultrahigh temperature (UHT) crustal metamorphism.This region has been the focus of long-standing collaborative research by the geologists who participated in the Australian National Antarctic Research Expeditions (ANARE) and the Japanese Antarctic Research Expeditions (JARE) and the Australian National Antarctic Research Expeditions (ANARE). It has been recognised internationally as a premier example of and type area for ultrahigh temperature (UHT) crustal metamorphism.

Until now, the only Antarctic site included in the IUGS Geological Heritage Sites was the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary on Seymour Island (Marambio Island). With the addition of these two sites, Antarctica now has a total of three sites on the list. This is the first time that sites involving Japan's Antarctic research program have been selected.

Descriptions of the two newly recognised sites, "Yamato Mountains Blue-Ice Meteorite Field" and "Archean Ultrahigh Temperature Metamorphism in the Napier Complex Antarctica," have been published in the IUGS publication *The Third 100 IUGS Geological Heritage Sites* as Site 292 and Site 243, respectively.

A. Yamaguchi and N. Imae (NIPR, Tokyo), 2026, Site 292: Yamato Mountains blue ice meteorite field,
S.L. Harley (Edinburgh, Scotland), T. Hokada (NIPR, Tokyo), E.S. Grew (Orono, USA), D. Dunkley (Warsaw, Poland), I.C.W. Fitzsimons (Perth, Australia), 2026, Site 243: Archean Ultrahigh Temperature Metamorphism in the Napier Complex
in L. Carcavilla, G. Lozano, A. Hilario, and S. Finney, eds, “The Third 100 IUGS Geological Heritage Sites”, IUGS (International Union of Geological Sciences), Zumaia, Spain, p. 254–255, ISBN: 978-8409923298.

Martian meteorite Yamato 000593 (13.7 kilograms) is the largest one found in the meteorite stranding zone south of Yamato Mountains (JARE-41).
